segments.text: Sorry, doctor, sorry I'm late. The car park out the front was chockers, so Linda dropped me at the door and then had to go hunting for a spot.
No dramas, you're here now. Take a seat, both of you. How have you been going since I saw you last week?
Honestly, not great. I've been worrying myself sick since you said the word pre-diabetes. Does that mean I'm definitely going to get diabetes?
That's a fair thing to be worried about, and I'm glad you asked it straight out. Tell me what's been on your mind.
Well, I keep reading things online and every site says something different. One says it's reversible, the next says it's a one-way street.
Dr Google does that to everyone. Here's the plain version. Your sugar level was a bit above normal, but well short of diabetes. Think of it as a yellow light, not a red one.
A yellow light. Okay. So what do I actually do at a yellow light?
We slow down and make some changes before it turns red. But first, how have you been feeling in yourself? Anything different lately?
Um, a bit tired, I suppose. Wiped out by mid-afternoon, which isn't like me at all.
Mm. And how long has the tiredness been hanging around?
About two weeks, I'd say. It started just before the blood test.
Oh, it's longer than that, love. It's been three weeks at least. You fell asleep in front of the footy the Saturday before your mum's birthday.
Was it? Maybe. I lose track of time when I'm stressed.
So somewhere between two and three weeks, then. We'll call it that and not argue over the calendar.
Now, have you been unusually thirsty, or getting up in the night to pass water?
No, nothing like that. I'm not up in the night at all, and I'm not thirsty any more than usual.
Good, that's reassuring. While we're chatting I'll read out your numbers from today.
Blood pressure is 132 over 84, which is fine, just a touch on the upper side. And you're 86 kilograms on the scales.
Is the weight a problem? I've put on a few kilos this year, I know, I know.
I just want to know what we can do at home, doctor. He won't stop fretting and it's wearing both of us out.
That's exactly the right question. From what we have so far, this looks like pre-diabetes, and it's been caught early, which is the best time to catch it.
Early. So it can go back to normal?
For many people, yes. Steady changes make the biggest difference. Walking for thirty minutes most days, and swapping sugary drinks for water. Nothing drastic.
Thirty minutes, I can do that. Do I need tablets for it?
Not at this stage. Let's see what the small changes do first.
And if I get it wrong? Slip up on a weekend or something?
Then you carry on Monday. One weekend doesn't undo anything. It's what happens over months that counts.
I'll walk with him in the evenings. Gives me an excuse to get out of the house anyway.
Lovely, that's a team effort. Now, I'd like to see you again in three months so we can see how things are travelling.
Three months. Right. Should I book that at the front?
Yes, the girls at the front desk will sort a time on your way out.
Thanks, doctor. Sorry again about being late, I'm a bit of a flustered mess today.
You've done well to ask your questions. Go easy on yourself, and on the internet.
Come on, love, let's find that car and have a walk down to the shops.
Righto. Cheers, doctor.
